subtitle: Reading the data, using the least-squares line, meaning of slope and intercept, and correlation

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct interpretation must attach the slope to the units of the study -- each additional hour of study is associated with a predicted increase of 6 points on the test -- and must be phrased as a prediction or an association, not as a guarantee that a particular student will gain 6 points.

traps.desc: computed predicted minus actual, reversing the sign of the residual

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct interpretation must say that about 94.6 percent of the variation in test scores among these six students is accounted for by the linear relationship with study hours, leaving about 5 percent to other causes. Full credit requires the words variation (or variability) and a reference to the scores, not merely repeating the number.

problems.slot: (a) the predicted score at zero hours

problems.desc: Part (b): a correct response must say that zero hours lies outside the range of study times actually observed, which runs from 1 to 6 hours, so the intercept of 50 is an extrapolation; it is the arithmetic value of the line at zero and not a trustworthy prediction of what a student who did not study would score.

Part (b): a correct response must say that a correlation of 0.97 measures only how closely the six points cluster about a line, and that a lurking variable such as prior preparation, sleep or motivation could raise both the study time and the score; observational data of this kind cannot establish that studying causes the higher score, and only a controlled experiment could.

Part (b): a correct response must say that 8 hours is beyond the largest observed study time of 6 hours, so the prediction of 98 is an extrapolation; there is no evidence the linear pattern continues, and the line would soon predict scores above 100, which the test cannot produce.

Part (b): a correct response must say that a residual of -12 means the new student scored 12 points below what the line predicts for 4 hours, far larger in size than any residual among the original six, whose largest was 3; adding such a point would scatter the data further from the line, lowering the correlation and pulling the fitted line downward near 4 hours.
